question: A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because she is seeing things that she knows are not there. Sometimes she sees a dog in her kitchen and at other times she sees a stranger in her garden, both of which no one else can see. She also reports a lack of motivation to do daily tasks for the past week. Three years ago, she was diagnosed with Parkinson disease and was started on levodopa and carbidopa. Her younger brother has schizophrenia. The patient also takes levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. She used to drink a bottle of wine every day, but she stopped drinking alcohol 2 months ago. Neurologic examination shows a mild resting tremor of the hands and bradykinesia. Her thought process is organized and logical. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Levodopa and carbidopa" -> "increased dopamine levels" -> "dopamine dysregulation" -> "visual hallucinations" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Alcohol cessation" -> "reduced GABAergic activity" -> "increased excitatory neurotransmission" -> "visual hallucinations" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Family history of schizophrenia" -> "genetic predisposition" -> "psychotic symptoms" -> "visual hallucinations" -> 50%
CHAIN: "Hypothyroidism" -> "levothyroxine treatment" -> "stable thyroid function" -> "unlikely cause of hallucinations" -> 30%
analysis: The patient's visual hallucinations are most likely due to an adverse effect of her Parkinson's disease medication, specifically levodopa and carbidopa. These medications can cause hallucinations, especially in older patients. Her organized thought process and the absence of other psychotic symptoms make schizophrenia less likely. Alcohol withdrawal is unlikely as she stopped drinking 2 months ago, and withdrawal symptoms typically occur within days to weeks after cessation. Major depressive disorder could explain her lack of motivation but not the hallucinations. Poorly controlled hypothyroidism is also unlikely to cause hallucinations.
